keyDates.appliesTo: RSA, ECDSA, finite-field DH/MQV, elliptic-curve DH/MQV

frameworks.criticalNuance: Larger classical key sizes do NOT extend the deadline. RSA-3072 and P-384 are disallowed after 2035 on the same schedule as RSA-2048 and P-256. The only difference is that 112-bit parameters get an earlier DEPRECATION milestone in 2030. Many vendors get this wrong.
frameworks.contextQuote: §4.1.1: SP 800-57pt1 had projected NIST would disallow 112-bit public-key schemes on 2031-01-01; IR 8547 instead DEPRECATES them at that level so organisations can continue use while migrating.
frameworks.customerFacingRule: Because this is a DRAFT, every customer-facing use must be labelled 'NIST draft guidance (IR 8547 ipd, November 2024)'. Presenting these as final binding dates is a factual error.

frameworks.name: Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography — Quantum Readiness: Cryptographic Discovery
documents: SP 1800-38A — Executive Summary (preliminary draft, comment closed 2023-06-08)
SP 1800-38B — Approach, Architecture, and Security Characteristics of Public Key Application Discovery Tools (preliminary draft, December 2023)
SP 1800-38C — Quantum Readiness: Testing Draft Standards for Interoperability and Performance (preliminary draft, December 2023)
frameworks.status: PRELIMINARY DRAFT — Volumes B and C comment period closed 2024-02-20. Additional volumes expected.
frameworks.role: THE MOST DIRECTLY RELEVANT NIST PUBLICATION TO THIS PRODUCT. Volume B is a practice guide for cryptographic discovery TOOLS — i.e. the exact product category Q-Vuln is in. It defines a discovery architecture, a normalisation scheme for discovery output, and a functional test plan for evaluating discovery tools.
frameworks.whyItMatters: IR 8547 tells us WHICH algorithms must go and by when. The CISA factsheet tells us inventory comes first. SP 1800-38B tells us HOW a discovery tool should be built and what it should emit. It is the closest thing to a specification for our product, and a buyer evaluating us may well use its functional test plan (Appendix C, eight use cases) as an evaluation rubric.

discoveryArchitecture.note: SP 1800-38B §4.1 defines three discovery domains. Our collector roadmap should map onto these explicitly.

domains.name: Protecting the Code Development Pipeline
domains.covers: CI/CD pipeline software, SDLC software, repository components

domains.name: Operational Systems and Applications
domains.covers: Filesystem scanning sensors on end-user devices and servers; EDR integration; BINARY scanning for third-party code with no available source
ourCollectors: B10 binaries — NOTE: NIST treats binary scanning as core, not deferred

domains.name: Transport Protocols and Network Services
domains.covers: Real-time network scanning and passive discovery from historical packet captures, across cloud, on-premises and untrusted networks

discoveryModalities.note: SP 1800-38B §4.1.4 names four ways discovery data is obtained. Our confidence model should distinguish them.

normalisationRequirement.note: DIRECT VALIDATION of our collector/observation design — and a concrete schema requirement we do not currently meet.
normalisationRequirement.problemQuote: §4.1.4: 'The reports produced by the discovery platforms in this demonstration are unique in that they do not use a common format for representing the discovery results. In a contrived example, a network discovery platform may identify a host system as host.example.com:443, whereas another may omit the port number (host.example.com). Therefore, we identified the need for a common format to represent normalized discovery reports, ideally by leveraging existing normalization efforts to the extent possible.'
normalisationRequirement.scopeNote: §4.1.4 explicitly states it 'does not define a schema, but instead defines descriptive data elements'. So this is guidance to align with, not a format to serialise to — CycloneDX CBOM remains our wire format.

networkDataElements.representation: String — IANA Service Name or TLS ALPN ID (RFC 6335 §5.1 / RFC 7301)
String — Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) 2.3, NIST IR 7695

normalisationRequirement.actionRequired: Our asset model uses a freeform jsonb locationDetail. To align, network-surface assets should carry these named elements with CPE 2.3 for software/OS/vendor identification. See open gap G-15.

consortiumMembers.note: COMMERCIAL REALITY CHECK. SP 1800-38B §5.1 lists the technology collaborators who contributed discovery tools to the NCCoE lab. These are the credible competitors in this exact category — not a spreadsheet.

frameworks.functionalTestPlan: Appendix C defines eight use cases for a Discovery Platform Lab Functional Demonstration. Worth treating as an acceptance-test suite for our own collectors, and as a likely buyer evaluation rubric.

frameworks.name: Quantum-Readiness: Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography
frameworks.tlp: TLP:CLEAR — may be shared without restriction
frameworks.role: The authoritative statement that quantum readiness begins with a cryptographic inventory. The structure our dashboard mirrors.
frameworks.CORRECTION: This document does NOT define a numbered five-stage roadmap. Earlier seed data in this repo invented one. The factsheet is organised into the NAMED SECTIONS listed below. Do not present numbered stages as quoted from CISA.

sections.heading: DISCUSS POST-QUANTUM ROADMAPS WITH TECHNOLOGY VENDORS

discoveryTargets.note: Under PREPARE A CRYPTOGRAPHIC INVENTORY, the factsheet names exactly three places cryptographic discovery tools should look. Our collector roadmap should map onto these explicitly.
targets: Network protocols, used to identify quantum-vulnerable algorithms in network protocols that allow traceability
Assets on end user systems and servers, including applications and associated libraries, both within application functionality and for firmware and software updates
Cryptographic code or dependencies in the continuous integration/continuous delivery development pipeline
discoveryTargets.embeddedCryptoWarning: Quoted: 'Discovery tools may not be able to identify embedded cryptography used internally within products, hindering discoverability or documentation. Organizations should ask vendors for lists of embedded cryptography within their products.' — PRIMARY-SOURCE SUPPORT for our coverage-gap panel (feature D3). CISA itself says tools have blind spots.

dataLifetimeSupport.note: PRIMARY-SOURCE SUPPORT for the X variable in Mosca (feature A3).
quotes: 'cyber threat actors could be targeting data today that would still require protection in the future (or in other words, has a long secrecy lifetime), using a catch now, break later or harvest now, decrypt later operation'

'Organizations should include in their inventory when and where quantum-vulnerable cryptography is being leveraged to protect the most sensitive and critical datasets and include estimates on length of protection for these datasets.'
'Prioritization should be given to high impact systems, industrial control systems (ICSs), and systems with long-term confidentiality/secrecy needs.'

frameworks.productNote: The inventory and prioritisation sections are what Q-Vuln automates. Vendor engagement is the vendor collector (B9). Roadmap establishment and migration execution are customer process we evidence but do not perform.
frameworks.retrievalNote: cisa.gov returns HTTP 403 to automated fetches; verified against the NIST NCCoE-hosted copy of the same factsheet.

frameworks.name: Migrating to Post-Quantum Cryptography (federal inventory mandate)
frameworks.role: Requires US federal civilian agencies to submit an annual prioritised cryptographic inventory. Defines a reporting FORMAT — our export must match it.
frameworks.corroboration: NIST IR 8547 §4 (line 432) states: 'National Security Memorandum 10 (NSM-10) establishes the year 2035 as the primary target' and refers to 'the overall goal of achieving widespread PQC adoption by 2035.' This corroborates the 2035 horizon from a verified NIST source.
frameworks.BLOCKER: The submission format and current status are NOT verified. whitehouse.gov/omb was not fetched. A human must confirm whether M-23-02 is superseded and obtain the current inventory submission template before we claim conformance.

frameworks.name: CycloneDX Cryptographic Bill of Materials
frameworks.role: The machine-readable interchange format for cryptographic inventory. Our primary export contract.
frameworks.capabilities: CBOM enables detailed representation of cryptographic assets — algorithms, keys and certificates — and their relationships to software components, to 'discover, manage, and report on cryptographic assets in preparation for a quantum-safe future'.
frameworks.CORRECTION: Seed data said 1.6 was current. It is not — 1.7 was released 2025-10-21. Target 1.7 for the CBOM exporter (feature A5/E3). Which version first introduced CBOM was not confirmed on the pages fetched; it is not needed to implement against 1.7.

frameworks.name: PCI DSS v4.0 Requirement 12.3.3
frameworks.role: Mandates a documented, annually-reviewed cryptographic inventory. Close to a literal description of this product.
frameworks.requirement: Cryptographic cipher suites and protocols in use are documented and reviewed at least once every 12 months, including: an up-to-date inventory of all cryptographic cipher suites and protocols in use (including purpose and where used); active monitoring of industry trends regarding continued viability; and a documented plan to respond to anticipated changes in cryptographic vulnerabilities.
frameworks.statusNote: Was future-dated best practice in PCI DSS 4.0; became mandatory after 2025-03-31, so it is IN FORCE now.
frameworks.commercialNote: Strongest commercial hook available for any card-handling customer — a mandated, recurring, documented cryptographic inventory with an explicit crypto-agility rationale. Build a PCI-specific report template.
frameworks.verificationNote: Consistent across multiple independent secondary sources but NOT verified against the PCI SSC primary document, which requires registration. A human must confirm exact wording and the 12.3.3 numbering in v4.0.1 before customer-facing use.

qDayScenarios.basis: NIST IR 8547 ipd deprecation milestone for 112-bit classical security, and NSA's indicative CNSA 2.0 equipment-transition completion date
NIST IR 8547 ipd disallowance date for ALL classical public-key algorithms, and the NSM-10 target year of 2035 as cited in IR 8547 §4
Slower-than-expected quantum hardware scaling. NOT derived from any published deadline — this is our own scenario and must be labelled as such.

qDayNote: These are REGULATORY deadlines, not predictions of when a cryptographically-relevant quantum computer will exist. That framing is both more defensible and more useful — compliance dates bind long before the physics does. The UI must say this explicitly rather than implying we know when Q-Day is. Note the 2030 and 2035 figures now trace to a verified primary source (IR 8547 ipd), but that source is a DRAFT.
